unclassifiedHead: {n} label(s) were counted that this page has no row for:
unclassifiedWhy: That is a call site somebody added without adding a row to DATA_CLASSES in admin-ui/encryption_admin.ts. It is drawn rather than dropped on purpose: the alternative is a table that goes on looking complete while the totals above it do not add up to the rows below.
noRotationModule: The data-key rotation module is not loaded in this process, so nothing here can be rotated.
rotationScheduled: Every data encryption key is rotated after {days} day(s) (keys.dataKeyRotationDays); a new key is used {lead} second(s) after it is published, and a replaced key is destroyed no sooner than {retire} day(s) after, once nothing is sealed under it.
rotationOff: Scheduled rotation is off: {reason}. A rotation by hand still works.
directoryCipher: Data stored in the directory is sealed with {cipher} (keys.directoryCipher); everything else with aes-256-gcm.
countedLast: What is sealed under each key is counted once a day (keys.data-key-count), last at {when}.
countedNotYet: What is sealed under each key is counted once a day (keys.data-key-count), and has not been counted yet.
noDataKey: No data encryption key is held yet: one is made the first time a value of its realm and class is sealed.
rotateNote: Each key gets a successor, used once it has been published; what the old key sealed is re-sealed by the re-encryption job.
reencryptNote: — re-seals what is still under a superseded key, and destroys a superseded key nothing is sealed under that has been superseded long enough.
countNote: — counts what is sealed under every key, in one pass of the store.
rotateKekNote: — the key management service makes a new version, and every data key is re-wrapped under it. The earlier version stays: data keys other nodes wrapped under it still unwrap. The identity this service runs as must be allowed to rotate the key, which the deployments here do not grant: they rotate it on the KMS's own schedule.
whatAnswers: This page answers what this service encrypts at rest, with which key, under which algorithm, and how much of it has happened. It is under Monitoring rather than beside the other two cryptography pages because of what it is:
whatDoes: says what this service does when it signs or encrypts and reads the same on a service that started a second ago, and
whatHolds: says what one realm holds. The numbers here go up while you watch.
whatNeither: Neither a sealed value nor an opened one appears on this page. A sealed value is a private key, an authenticator’s shared secret or somebody’s recovery codes, and printing either half of one would hand over exactly what the sealing exists to protect. Its only controls rotate the data encryption keys, re-seal and count what they sealed, and rotate a key-encryption key that is in a key management service (which makes the new version itself), and they show nothing. A key-encryption key READ into this process is rotated by deploying its successor — this service reads one and never writes one — and a decrypt this button would be the one door onto material no door is supposed to have.
whatTitle: What this page is, and the two things it deliberately has not got
keyReadBy: The key-encryption key is read by common/secrets.js from
keyKms: , which never leaves it: the service holds a handle, not the key, and asks it to wrap and unwrap each data key
keyOnce: , once, at startup and before the listener binds. file is the default because it needs nothing: Kubernetes mounts a Secret as a file, Docker mounts a secret as a file, and every other provider here is that same idea with somebody else’s access control in front of it.
keyShort: A key shorter than 32 bytes is REFUSED rather than stretched. Stretching would let a four-character password protect every signing key this service holds while the log said AES-256. Hex is tried before base64, because a 64-character hex string is also valid base64 and reading it that way produces 48 different bytes.
